newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian group says it killed top union leader.
newsitem.headline: Algerian group says it killed top union leader.

text.p: A Moslem guerrilla faction claimed responsibility for the killing of Algerian union leader Abdelhak Benhamouda, whose death was mourned on Saturday by Algerians who staged a one-day work stoppage in his memory.
The Algerian Jihad Islamic Front (FIDA), which is widely believed to be a small Moslem guerrilla group operating mainly in Algiers, said it carried out Tuesday's shooting.

"The FIDA announces its responsibility in the attack which targeted Abdelhak Benhamouda, a man who placed himself in the service of the military junta," said a FIDA statement carried by leading Algerian newspapers on Saturday.
In the statement, signed by the group's military commander in Algiers, Ahmed Abu Elfida, the group vowed to stage more attacks against the government and its supporters.

A better-known Algerian guerrilla group, Armed Islamic Group (GIA), has also warned it will kill more Algerian personalities, residents said, quoting GIA warnings pasted on walls recently in the Algerian capital.
Employees in Algeria, except for those in emergency services like hospitals, stayed away from work on Saturday to mourn Benhamouda, Union Generale des Travailleurs Algeriens (UGTA) officials said.
Benhamouda was secretary-general of the UGTA, Algeria's one-million-strong workers' union umbrella.
Schoolchildren were sent home on Saturday morning and main offices and shops were closed in Algiers, said residents speaking by telephone.
State-run radio and television stations said most of the country's nearly five million workers observed the stoppage.

President Liamine Zeroual, in a move dismissing guerrilla threats, on Saturday invited legal opposition parties for talks on parliamentary elections planned for the first half of this year, his office said in a statement.
The talks would be held on February 11 to discuss the formation of an independent committee to oversee the polls, said the statement carried by the official Algerian news agency APS.
"The meeting will be an occasion to exchange views on all other questions related to this significant election," the presidential statement added.
Algeria has been without an elected parliament since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a huge lead.
The Algerian government bars the now outlawed FIS from fielding candidates to run in the next parliamentary polls.

Almost all Algerian newspapers carried a torrent of questions on Benhamouda's murder, just weeks after he had announced he would form a political party, and the escape of the killers in the heavily policed Algerian capital.
They questioned who really killed him, or ordered his elimination, fuelling doubts the assassins were Moslem guerrillas.
Benhamouda was given a martyr's funeral on Thursday, attended by President Zeroual and senior government figures.

Shortly afterwards, Algerian security forces reported that a "terrorist" -- Algeria's official term for Moslem fundamentalists -- had killed retired general Habib Khelil in the western Algerian city of Oran.
El Watan newspaper said on Saturday a gunman shot Khelil in the head while he was shopping at a market, and then a second gunman shot him twice in the head as the former general was collapsing.
Suspected Moslem guerrillas killed eight people, including a baby on Wednesday night or Thursday morning in Sidi Kaddour hamlet, some 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, Algerian security forces said.

According to official figures, nearly 200 people have been killed in Algeria in massacres and bomb attacks since the Moslem fasting month Ramadan started on January 10. Algerian newspapers put the figure at more than 250.

About 60,000 people have been killed since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election which Islamists were set to win. A new general election is promised in the first half of this year.
